claims.text: An integrated high-throughput workflow coupling CALPHAD phase predictions with DFT mechanical-property calculations can predict intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight RHEA compositions.
The workflow can identify regions where Ti or Al substitutes for heavier elements while preserving a beneficial single-phase or controlled dual-phase microstructure.
A beneficial single-phase or controlled dual-phase microstructure can promote both strength and ductility in RHEAs.
The candidate initial state is a disordered single-phase or near-single-phase BCC refractory HEA.
Typical candidate RHEAs have high density and may contain brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Candidate RHEAs can subsequently be synthesized and processed using powder-based or additive-manufacturing routes.
Controlled coherent secondary-phase precipitation can provide substantial strengthening while retaining appreciable tensile ductility.
Formation of a Laves-type secondary phase can increase hardness and yield strength in a BCC RHEA.
Laves-type precipitation contributes to both strengthening and improved ductility.
Lattice-distortion features enhance dislocation interactions and provide solid-solution strengthening.
Local chemical-ordering features can alter dislocation mobility and provide additional strengthening.
Incorporating lightweight refractory elements lowers alloy density while maintaining high melting points.
Optimized precipitation and lattice features improve the balance of dislocation mobility, producing both high yield strength and ductility.
Computationally selected and synthesized RHEAs will have significantly higher specific strength than conventional RHEAs.
Computationally selected and synthesized RHEAs will have improved ductility relative to conventional RHEAs.
Conventional RHEAs often rely on heavy elements and therefore have high density.
Conventional RHEAs may develop brittle intermetallic phases and generally have limited ductility.
Success is limited to a compositional window in which lightweight elements do not destabilize the desired phase constitution or reduce high-temperature strength.
Outside the successful compositional window, unstable phases or inadequate mechanical properties may result.
A greater than 10% increase in specific strength, together with improved ductility and reduced density relative to a conventional-RHEA control, is the proposed decisive success criterion.
